title: He Thought About Rome Every Day
text:
The year was 1764, and Edward Gibbon was 27, headed for Rome on his Grand Tour. He had traversed the Alps from France not on a mule but in a chair carried between poles by porters. (He was “no great jockey,” a companion noted.) Gibbon then made his way through Turin and Milan, paused in Florence, and, as autumn set in, continued south. Crossing the Tiber, his destination now in sight, he was overcome.

 “I can neither express nor forget the strong emotions which agitated my mind as I first approached and entered the eternal city,” Gibbon recalled years later in a memoir. “After a sleepless night I trod, with a lofty step, the ruins of the Forum; each memorable spot where Romulus stood or Tully spoke or Caesar fell was at once present to my eye; and several days of intoxication were lost or enjoyed before I could descend to a cool and minute investigation.”

 Gibbon loved his rhetorical couplings—those harnessed pairs of verbs or adjectives that are sometimes at odds (“lost or enjoyed,” “express nor forget”), pulling the reader in different directions, as the critic Clive James once observed . The oddest pairing of all is that of Gibbon himself and his monumental work, The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire , which he began writing seven years after that first (and only) visit to Rome. Gibbon was, by his own description, “puny”—4 feet 7 inches tall. His masterpiece is towering, a million and a half words published over the course of little more than a decade. The first of the six volumes—an immediate best seller in Britain—appeared the same year as the Declaration of Independence and The Wealth of Nations .

 There was no real precedent for what Gibbon had achieved. The Decline and Fall was an attempt to write history in a way we now take for granted : that is, by seeking to explain what actually happened. Gibbon was neither an annalist nor a zealot. He had arguments to make—about the unrivaled stability and happiness enjoyed for a spell by the Roman empire’s subjects, about the defeat of liberty by despotism and decadence, about the corrosive effects of corruption and Christianity—but his account is not subservient to them. He is often imprecise, as well as confident in his imagination. But he also weighs evidence. He compares cultures. He shifts perspective.

 Gibbon’s appetite for written sources was gargantuan and his knowledge of them profound, though he did not bring a modern critical faculty to their interpretation. He was an impresario, not a pedant—judicious, skeptical, and ironic, with a taste for drama. And the writing! At times so over-egged as to make Henry James seem like Hemingway, but seductive in its rhythms and illuminated by epigrammatic flashes: “A good soldier should dread his own officers far more than the enemy.” “Revenge is profitable, gratitude is expensive.” The narrative is at once sweeping and detailed—equal parts Balzac and Trollope, George Lucas and TMZ.

 The Decline and Fall ’s influence has been immense. The work created the basic storyline of Roman history , from “good emperors” to barbarians, and for generations has shaped an understanding of imperial ruin as “the natural and inevitable effect of immoderate greatness.” It captivated newly independent America, whose Founders cherished republican government but feared that the Roman past held danger signs. People continue to explore its claims and insights, as well as the experiences that shaped its author: Was Gibbon a fatalist or, living at the core of a young empire himself , an optimist? Whatever the answer, his eyes seem to follow us around the room.

 Gibbon the man is a figure, as Martha Saxton writes in her posthumously published The Conversions of Edward Gibbon: A Modern Biography , who appears almost laughably devoid of the majesty his prose leads you to expect. As a boy, his ungainly body and unhappy experiences with peers left him deeply insecure and drove him to books. In later life, he grew obese and suffered from a hydrocele—a scrotal swelling—that further hampered his movement. He was vain and foppish, with a habit of waving his snuffbox didactically when he wanted to make a point. People acknowledged his brilliance but also made him an object of ridicule and even contempt. James Boswell, who knew Gibbon as a member of the Club, a literary group that included Samuel Johnson, described him as an “ugly, affected, disgusting fellow.”

 Saxton, a feminist historian and for many years a professor at Amherst College, is the author of acclaimed biographies of Jayne Mansfield, Louisa May Alcott, and Mary Ball Washington (the mother of George). She came to Gibbon from an unusual angle, her attention drawn initially by the notable misogyny of the Decline and Fall . Powerful women are painted as gorgons or succubi. The few whom Gibbon approves of are described as possessing “manly” virtues. In Gibbon’s lexicon, decadence is often a synonym for effeminacy .

 But Saxton’s response to Gibbon is complicated. She describes herself as both repelled by his venom and dazzled by the Decline and Fall —by its writing, scope, and command, and by the mark it left. She also finds Gibbon’s misogyny baffling. Male writers of the Enlightenment were eager to engage a female audience. Gibbon himself enjoyed close friendships with several women, in particular an aunt, Catherine Porten, who first cultivated “a taste for books, which is still the pleasure and glory of my life.” Aunt Kitty would be Gibbon’s friend and counselor for nearly four decades.

 Saxton doesn’t have a ready explanation for Gibbon’s attitudes, and doesn’t try to force one. Instead, she broadens her inquiry to explore the inner life of a man who repeatedly broke with convention—the “conversions” of her title—only to scramble back to safer ground. A lonely misfit emerges from her book, confident in his abilities but wounded in his soul, who escapes into a world of words as the only place where he can exercise complete control. Saxton is hardly protective of her subject, but she also has no patience for the cruelty of men like Boswell, whose remarks about Gibbon give her “much sympathy for the tiny, affected, brilliant, scarred man.”

 [ From the January 1878 issue: William Dean Howells on Edward Gibbon ] 

 Gibbon was born in South London in 1737 to a family of wealth and property. Though sickly himself, he was the only one of seven children to survive infancy. His unloving mother died when he was 10. His difficult father was a stern traditionalist who kept a tight hold on money and behavior. Young Edward was sent away for schooling. The most significant event from Gibbon’s brief time at Oxford was his rebellious embrace of Catholicism—not a route to advancement in 18th-century Britain.

 He was sent to stay with a Calvinist pastor and his family in Lausanne, Switzerland. The prospect of disinheritance proved to be a potent theology. As Gibbon later wrote, “The various articles of the Romish creed disappeared like a dream.” But the five years spent in Lausanne also made him a French-speaking child of the Enlightenment, with continental manners and republican values. He took inspiration from the Swiss fight for democracy—a movement, he once wrote, from which “the dullest stranger would catch fire.” He acquired habits of reading and study that he never relinquished. Lausanne was also where he met an intellectually intrepid young woman named Suzanne Curchod and embarked on the one romantic adventure of his life. But his father refused to bless their engagement—Suzanne had no wealth and no desire to live in England—and Gibbon broke it off. “I sighed as a lover,” he recalled years later. “I obeyed as a son.”

 In fact, he did more than obey. Returning home, he made a kind of peace with his father, slipped into a caricature of Englishness, and adopted the macho swagger of his class. By way of reward, he was eventually permitted to embark on his Grand Tour.

 In Saxton’s telling, every time Gibbon ventures into the realm of possibility, he finds his way back to a more comfortable and conventional path. After taking a seat in Parliament—a chamber then being roused by the voices of Edmund Burke and Charles James Fox—he sat silently for years, forgoing even the formality of a maiden speech. In his votes, the youthful idealist who had applauded the republican virtues of Switzerland opposed American independence and supported the pro-war policies of Lord North and King George III, though with more detachment than passion. The main interest he showed in Britain’s corrupt society—the rotten boroughs, the pervasive grift—was how to secure a comfortable place in it. He set himself up handsomely in London, hiring servants, dining at Boodle’s, consorting with blue bloods.

 The single conviction to which Gibbon held true all his life was that he should write. The world he conjured with his pen was a world where he felt assured and free, and he seems to have recognized this early. In his memoir, Gibbon recalled a teenage ambition to embark on a historical study, subject matter unclear: “Unprovided with original learning, unformed in the habits of thinking, unskilled in the arts of composition, I resolved to write a book.” He pursued this ambition in fits and starts until, one night during that visit to Rome in 1764, he found the inspiration for his life’s work.

 [ Read: The brain of a man who is always thinking about ancient Rome ] 

 Gibbon’s description of the moment is famous. In his embellished recollection, the idea for the Decline and Fall sprang to mind “as I sat musing amidst the ruins of the Capitol, while the barefooted friars were singing vespers in the temple of Jupiter.” He did not start writing seriously until 1771, a year after his father died and he at last came into his inheritance. He was 34 years old, and more than half his life was gone. With remarkable speed, he produced six volumes. The first three covered the period from the peak of the Pax Romana, in the first and second centuries C.E.—“the period in the history of the world, during which the condition of the human race was most happy and prosperous”—through the collapse of the Western empire, in the fifth century. The last three volumes, at a gallop, covered the next millennium, up to the fall of Constantinople. The original full set weighed 30 pounds.

 Within the walls of his study on Bentinck Street, in London, Gibbon was an omnipotent ruler, dispatching emperors, summoning invaders, hurling judgments. He looks beneath and beyond the golden age to depict a Roman world of violence, injustice, excess, and caprice. Gibbon’s wit, stentorian but sly, is allowed to unfold slowly. Of one emperor, he wrote, “Twenty-two acknowledged concubines, and a library of sixty-two thousand volumes, attested the variety of his inclinations, and from the productions he left behind him, it appears that the former as well as the latter were designed for use rather than ostentation.” Gibbon pioneered the use of footnotes, which he deployed by the thousands to raise a hackle, settle a score, or supply a punch line.

 Volume I of the Decline and Fall , published in 1776, sold out quickly. As more volumes appeared, Gibbon’s celebrity grew. He was corpulent now, the target of jokes about his own immoderate greatness. But Gibbon labored on, coming to “the last lines of the last page” with, he recalled, a sense of satisfaction: When he finally laid down his pen and strolled the grounds of his home, “all Nature was silent.”

 Martha Saxton died in 2023, her book not yet finished. Her daughter, Josephine Saxton Ferorelli, describes in a foreword her mother’s career and her deepening interest in Gibbon’s tortured character—a man who could neither open his heart nor look into it. In an afterword, Saxton’s friend, the critic Judith Thurman, who edited the book, outlines some of the themes that Saxton never fully addressed. Saxton is a superb writer, and the 200 or so pages that she completed have an essayistic flavor. She tells stories and thinks aloud. But the biography stops abruptly with an account of Gibbon’s death. It’s missing some of the critical reflections on the Decline and Fall —including its relevance to the world today—that Saxton had been saving for the end.

 [ Listen: The David Frum Show with Mary Beard on why America isn’t Rome ] 

 The fact that Saxton’s book is unfinished gives it a haunting dimension. What would have come next? We have some clues. Many passages in The Conversions of Edward Gibbon point to big questions on her mind, if not always to what her answers would be. As Thurman explains, Saxton also left behind working notes for the final part of the book. In so many ways, Saxton’s biography is built around tensions: between finished and unfinished; between Gibbon the man and Gibbon the historian; between past and present.

 A question that Saxton raises more than once has to do with values. “Gibbon apparently didn’t see a contradiction, or at least feel a moral scruple, in revering and serving the British Empire while loathing the Roman one,” Saxton writes. “He decried Roman corruption, but he wasn’t interested in reforming his own corrupt government.” He was not blind to the parallels. “When we want to paint the most distant centuries,” he wrote to Suzanne Curchod after Volume I was published, “we end up drawing them, without realizing it, based on the models we have in front of our eyes.” Was he nothing more than a hypocrite? Saxton resists a simple verdict. In his writing, he is unsparing about human nature; in his life, he is desperate for acceptance. It’s a discordant but not uncommon coupling—like one of Gibbon’s harnessed pairs.

 A larger question involves Gibbon’s legacy. In the closing lines of the last volume, Gibbon underscored the grim majesty of his subject matter. The destruction of the Roman empire, he wrote, had been “the greatest, perhaps, and most awful scene in the history of mankind.” The Decline and Fall has been holding up a mirror ever since, inviting readers to see their own world in an ancient one. Historians and critics, along with the architects of America’s imperium, have wrestled with Gibbon for a quarter of a millennium. Does Rome’s fate offer useful guidance? Can it prompt reforms and prevent mistakes? Are all empires doomed?

 Gibbon himself was both wistful about the Roman empire’s impermanence and clear-eyed about its often monstrous nature. Wistfulness, filtered through the gauzy lens of the Romantics, continues to color popular attitudes; the sight of a broken column beneath the umbrella pines may still elicit a sigh. But it can be a good thing when empires die, and it was definitely a good thing that this one did. None of us would want to live in the imperial-Roman world—a world based on slavery and steeped in terror, with no concept of human equality or true democracy.

 Gibbon died in 1794, perhaps the result of an infection after surgery to relieve his hydrocele. He hadn’t had much to say about what the future might hold, but he’d been fatalistic about the ills that bring down empires—they were “natural and inevitable.” He had seen Britain lose its American colonies, though he harbored no animus toward the Americans themselves and even thought they might one day come in handy.

 [ From the April 2021 issue: No, really, are we Rome? ] 

 At one point in the Decline and Fall , Gibbon steps back—poking his head out from the page as he sometimes would—and reflects on the cultured and wealthy Europe that had emerged after centuries of darkness. He admires what he sees: “our general state of happiness, the system of arts, and laws, and manners.” Would barbarism ever return? Yes, some “savage conqueror” might one day ride forth from “the deserts of Tartary.” The foe would of course be met by “the numerous armies of Germany, the gallant nobles of France, and the intrepid freemen of Britain.” These groups might even “confederate for their common defence.” But despite best efforts, he concedes, the challenge could prove too great.

 Gibbon does not worry. Driven back to the beaches, the plucky remnant of defenders would have one more chance: They could board “ten thousand vessels” for the beckoning New World across the ocean, where Europeans had already begun to live. Freedom, justice, progress—they would surely be safe in America.

 This article appears in the January 2027 print edition with the headline “He Thought About Rome Every Day.”
